title: How to rotate your SSH keys without locking yourself out
excerpt: Add the new key first, test it, then remove the old one.
textContent:
Rotating SSH keys is routine maintenance, but doing the steps in the wrong order can lock you out of a server. This guide takes about ten minutes. You need shell access to the server with your current key.

Step 1: Generate a new key on your laptop. Run ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "laptop-2026" and accept the default file location. Set a passphrase.

Step 2: Add the new public key to the server. Run ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub user@server. This appends the key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys without removing the old one.

Step 3: Test the new key in a second terminal before you change anything else. Run ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 user@server. Keep your original session open until this works.

Step 4: Remove the old key. On the server, open ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and delete the line that ends with your old key's comment. Save the file.

Step 5: Confirm the old key is rejected. From your laptop, run ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa user@server. It should fail with "Permission denied (publickey)."

Common mistakes: deleting the old key before testing the new one, and editing authorized_keys with a tool that changes its permissions. The file should stay at mode 600.

You're done when the new key logs in and the old key is refused.
